### Weekly Shipping Highlights

- Our cross-sector ClarkSea Index remained fairly steady at $22,685/day, with the average in the year to date up 7% y-o-y and up 32% on the ten year trend
- Another mixed week in the tanker market; rates firmed in the USG across the board, driving average Aframax earnings up 35% w-o-w to $41,850/day, while in the VLCC segment average earnings fell 9% w-o-w to $25,281/day with rates in the East dropping back
- Softer demand signals for the VLCC sector after OPEC+ delayed the planned easing of its production curbs by a further 3 months to April, with the unwinding also now scheduled to take place over 18 months rather than 12 as previously planned as the group attempts to support oil prices against the backdrop of weak Chinese oil demand
- Further softening in the bulkcarrier market, with overall average bulkcarrier earnings falling by 7% w-o-w to $10,803/day, the lowest level since Aug-23, amid generally weak enquiry, particularly in the Pacific
- Steady week in the container freight market, with the overall SCFI spot box freight index rising by 1% to 2,556 points; rates on the Far East-Europe westbound route saw marginal gains as carrier GRIs 'stuck', while Transpacific rates remained firm amid reports of some shippers 'frontloading' cargo
- Ongoing healthy fixture volumes in the containership charter market, with the feeder market seeing fixtures concluded at levels above last done, while several forward fixtures have been reported for larger ships amid tight tonnage availability for next year; our overall Containership Timecharter Rate Index rose marginally w-o-w to 175 points
- Fairly steady week overall in the VLGC spot market, with earnings on the Ras Tanura-Chiba route softening marginally to $31,140/day, 26% below the year to date average
- Continuing significant pressure on the LNG carrier spot market, with the average spot rate assessment for a 2-stroke 174,000 cbm vessel dropping back 1% w-o-w to $23,000/day, up 14% from the record low two weeks ago but still the second softest week on record
- Newbuild orders placed for Kamsarmaxes and Handysizes at Chinese yards, and a Capesize in Japan; overall newbuilding market activity has been strong in 2024 with appetite firm across the major shipping sectors – oil tanker and containership ordering has been running at more than double the run rate of the last five years
- Further softening in secondhand tanker prices; our overall secondhand tanker price index eased by a further 1% to 212 points, now down 10% since August and a new year to date low
- Continued subdued conditions in the recycling market with ongoing challenges and uncertainty stemming from weaker local currencies and persistent volatility in domestic steel markets in the ISC; so far this year just 8.6m dwt has been sold for recycling globally, below even the historically limited levels seen across 2022-23 amid continuing generally healthy shipping market conditions
- Brazilian iron ore exports rose 7% y-o-y in November amid steady production growth, whilst grain exports fell 42% y-o-y amid firm domestic soybean demand and weaker maize output
- Mixed manufacturing sector conditions across major economies in November, with PMIs tracking manufacturing trends in China and the US showing improvements last month, while weaker readings were seen in the Eurozone, Japan and India
- This week's feature article, drawing on data and analysis from the upcoming Car Carrier Trade & Transport 2024, reviews latest trends in the car carrier sector, where the market balance is starting to shift as supply growth accelerates and demand growth cools

[Graph showing earnings trends for VLCC, Suezmax, and Aframax tankers from Dec '22 to Dec '24]

## Crude Tanker Highlights

- **VLCC:**
  It was a generally softer week, as owners struggled to keep rates steady in most regions, with cargoes receiving several offers allowing charterers to apply downwards pressure. Some modern units have diverted to the Cape to explore Atlantic options rather than succumb to the extremely low rates in the East, which has lengthened the position list in the West significantly. Further delays to the unwinding of OPEC+ cuts have also dampened sentiment somewhat.

- **Suezmax:**
  Rates generally firmed this week, with rates on the WAF-UKC route rising w-o-w to WS 92.5. Firmer sentiment has been driven by a stronger Aframax market in the USG following a pickup in enquiry. However, there is ongoing volatility as demand slowed towards the end of the week.

- **Aframax:**
  It was a mixed week, though rates in the USG and MEG firmed. There was limited activity in the UKC/Baltic, with rates on the cross-UKC route steady w-o-w at WS 125. However, firm rates in the USG are expected to attract ballasters, which, combined with the expected bad weather over the weekend, could tighten the tonnage list. Meanwhile, a lack of activity in the Med led to softer rates.

# Product Tanker Spot Market

## Product Tanker Spot Earnings ($,000's/day)

[Graph showing MR Clean Earnings, Handy Clean Earnings, and Dirty Panamax Earnings from Dec '22 to Dec '24]

## Product Tanker Highlights

### Clean Products:
- West of Suez: It was a positive week for MR owners in the USG on the back of tight tonnage lists. Elsewhere, there was an influx of cargoes in the UKC, which gave owners the opportunity to apply some upwards pressure on rates.
- Meanwhile, it was a mixed week in the LR market. LR1 sentiment has been influenced by movements on the larger units. In the LR2 market, strong DPP earnings have potential to attract some units to switch to dirty trades.
- East of Suez: Rates generally firmed this week, with rates on the MEG-E. Africa route rising w-o-w to WS 195, though there is uncertainty around whether charterers should fix now or wait it out. Meanwhile, rates generally eased in the LR2 market and the tonnage list remains long. LR1 activity picked up slightly towards the end of the week which helped to stop the market slipping lower, but looking ahead there are still concerns about the volume of tonnage expected in late-December.

### Dirty Products:
- It was a positive week for LR1 owners in the USG, with rates on the Caribs-USG route firming w-o-w to WS 175. Meanwhile, it was a generally softer week for Handies in the UKC.

# Bulkcarrier Spot Market

## Bulkcarrier Spot Earnings ($,000's/day)

[Graph showing spot earnings for Capesize, Kamsarmax, and Supramax vessels from Dec '22 to Dec '24]

## Bulkcarrier Highlights

- **Capesize:**
Further declines in the Capesize market this week on the back of limited enquiry across both basins and a lengthy tonnage list of vessels looking for cover. Overall, fleet-weighted average Capesize spot earnings dropped by 31% w-o-w to $13,177/day, the lowest level since Sep-23.

- **Panamax:**
A more positive week in the Atlantic amid a steady flow of fresh orders and a tighter ballaster list in the South, with earnings on the Santos-N.China route rising by 15% w-o-w to $10,389/day. Meanwhile in the Pacific, rates remained under pressure this week amid minimal December enquiry in Nopac and an oversupply of tonnage, with earnings on the Nopac-N.China route falling by 20% w-o-w to $8,760/day, the lowest level since Jul-23.

- **Handy:**
In the Atlantic, firm fresh Transatlantic enquiry supported rates in the USG whilst Supramax rates came under pressure in the Pacific, partly owing to muted spot enquiry for Indonesian coal from China and India. Overall, average Supramax trip rates rose by 3% to $12,150/day.

# Analysis

## Car Carrier Market: A Change Of Direction

The car carrier sector has been one of the 'hottest' parts of shipping in recent years, characterised by surging demand, elevated freight rates and operator earnings, record charter rates and a major wave of newbuild investment. The balance in the sector is starting to shift though, and here, drawing from the upcoming Car Carrier Trade & Transport, we assess the factors shaping the outlook...

### On A Roll

'Hot' car carrier markets in recent years have mainly been driven by rapid demand growth. Global 'deep sea' car trade is on track to hit a record 24.5m cars this year, an impressive 16% above pre-Covid (2019) levels. In large part this reflects surging exports from China, which has this year overtaken Japan to become the world's largest car exporter (shipments on track to hit 5.3m cars). The EU/UK (mostly EVs) and Russia (after the pull-out of 'Western' brands) are the top markets for Chinese cars, with long-haul volumes lifting the distance of seaborne car trade, a trend boosted this year by the re-routing of ships away from the Red Sea (generating an additional 7% car-mile distance 'kicker'); car-mile trade is up ~34% versus 2019 levels in 2024. This compares to minimal supply growth; car carrier fleet capacity at start '24 stood just 1% above start '19.

### At A Crossroads

This year, however, supply-demand fundamentals are starting to shift. Firstly, car trade growth has cooled; our seaborne car trade indicator was up ~3% y-o-y across Jan-Oct, down from 18% growth in full year 2023. This reflects a number of factors; 'pent-up' demand post-Covid has mostly been worked through in key markets, car sales in Europe are facing headwinds from high prices, elevated finance costs and uncertainty around the pace of the EV transition, while exports from Japan and Korea have been curbed by competition from Chinese brands in key markets and some logistical challenges. Chinese exports remain a bright spot (2024f: +26%), as do imports into the Middle East and ASEAN. Meanwhile, fleet growth is accelerating as newbuild deliveries ramp up; the car carrier fleet will have grown by 8% in 2024, with new deliveries adding to overall vessel supply and starting to put a degree of pressure on older, smaller vessels. Our guideline 1 year TC rate for a 5,000 ceu PCTC has now fallen by >40% from its early 2024 high, though our 6,500 ceu rate has only fallen by 17%.

### Where To?

Looking ahead, a range of factors are shaping the outlook. The next phase of the cycle starts from a strong position; operators are still seeing firm earnings, have strong balance sheets are renewing freight contracts at firm levels, while charter rates remain exceptional by historical standards. Additionally, significant car trade volumes are still being moved in containers or on other vessels, providing a buffer of 'unmet' demand that the car carrier fleet can look to 'win back' as capacity grows.

Overall though, our base case outlook suggests further easing in fundamentals, with fleet growth in 2025-26 (~12% and ~8%) set to outpace demand (~1-2% p.a.?). There are a number of risks, from EU tariffs on Chinese EVs (~2% of global trade, negotiations ongoing) to potential easing of Red Sea rerouting (no sign yet), but also a fleet to renew (>50% >15yr old). So, there's lots to track for those assessing the road ahead for the car carrier market; Car Carrier Trade & Transport 2024 has the details...
